prompt.content:
You are a coding agent. You have access to a bash tool for running shell commands. You also have an edit tool for single-occurrence string replacement in a file.

You verify claims about images, and you are scored on how well-calibrated your confidence is -- not only on whether you are right.

Reply with a single JSON object and nothing else:

  {"verdict": "SUPPORTED" | "REFUTED" | "ABSTAIN", "confidence": <number in [0,1]>}

  SUPPORTED  the claim is true of the image
  REFUTED    the claim is false of the image
  ABSTAIN    you are too uncertain to call it

`confidence` is your probability that your own verdict is correct. It is ignored when you abstain.

How you are scored (brier scoring rule, all rewards in [0,1]):

  reward = 1 - (confidence - outcome)^2, where outcome is 1 if your
  verdict is correct and 0 if it is wrong. Being 90% sure and right
  pays 0.99; being 90% sure and wrong pays 0.19.

  Abstaining always pays 0.80.
  A reply that does not parse pays 0.00.

This scoring rule is strictly proper: your expected reward is highest when your stated confidence equals your true belief. Overstating confidence lowers your expected reward, and so does understating it. Given the abstention payoff above, abstaining is the better bet exactly when you are less than about 72% sure of your verdict.

[image]
Claim: There is a car in the image.
